questions.q: State the Work-Energy Theorem and define each term.
questions.a: The net work done by all forces acting on a body equals the change in its kinetic energy: W_net = delta_KE = (1/2)mv^2 - (1/2)mu^2, where W_net is net work (joules), m is mass (kg), v is final velocity (m/s), and u is initial velocity (m/s). A wrong answer (e.g., "work equals energy") is too vague — it must specify that NET work equals CHANGE in kinetic energy, with the formula.

questions.q: A 2 kg object accelerates from 4 m/s to 8 m/s. Calculate the net work done on it.
questions.a: W_net = delta_KE = (1/2)(2)(8^2) - (1/2)(2)(4^2) = (1)(64) - (1)(16) = 64 - 16 = 48 J. The net work done is 48 joules. A wrong answer (e.g., (1/2)(2)(8-4)^2 = 8 J) uses the difference of velocities squared incorrectly — the formula is (1/2)mv^2 - (1/2)mu^2, not (1/2)m(v-u)^2.

questions.q: A net force of 10 N acts on a 2 kg object over a distance of 5 m. The object starts from rest. Find the final velocity using the Work-Energy Theorem.
questions.a: Step 1: Calculate work. W = F * d = 10 * 5 = 50 J. Step 2: Apply theorem. W = delta_KE = (1/2)mv^2 - (1/2)mu^2. Since u = 0: 50 = (1/2)(2)v^2 = v^2. So v^2 = 50, v = 7.07 m/s. A wrong answer (e.g., v = 10 m/s from a = F/m = 5, v = at without time) uses kinematics without the theorem.

questions.q: A 3 kg object moving at 6 m/s is brought to rest by friction. Calculate the work done by friction.
questions.a: W_net = delta_KE = (1/2)(3)(0^2) - (1/2)(3)(6^2) = 0 - 27 = -27 J. The work done by friction is -27 J (negative because friction opposes motion, reducing kinetic energy). A wrong answer (e.g., +27 J) misses the sign — friction does negative work because it reduces kinetic energy.

questions.q: Why is the work done by friction negative? Explain using the Work-Energy Theorem.
questions.a: Friction acts opposite to the direction of motion, so the angle between force and displacement is 180 degrees, and W = Fd cos(180) = -Fd. By the Work-Energy Theorem, W_net = delta_KE. Since friction reduces kinetic energy (object slows down), delta_KE is negative, so W_net is negative. The negative work reflects that friction removes kinetic energy from the object (converting it to heat). A wrong answer (e.g., "friction is negative because it is bad") confuses a value judgment with the mathematical sign.

questions.q: A student claims: "If no work is done on an object, its kinetic energy is zero." Evaluate this statement.
questions.a: The statement is incorrect. The Work-Energy Theorem says W_net = delta_KE (change in kinetic energy), not W_net = KE (kinetic energy itself). If no work is done (W_net = 0), then delta_KE = 0, meaning the kinetic energy does not change — the object continues at the same velocity. An object moving at constant velocity has non-zero kinetic energy but zero change in kinetic energy, so zero net work. A wrong evaluation (agreeing with the student) confuses "change in KE" with "KE itself."
